Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space. An **unnormalized target density** is a measurable function $\tilde p:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$Z_p:=\int_{\mathsf X}\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
The target probability measure is $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$. A **proposal density** is a measurable $q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\int q\,d\mu=1$; write $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. The input integrand $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, and the input sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is IID with law $Q$, in the sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. The normalizing constant $Z_p$ is known for this algorithm.

**Admissible conditions for an unbiased estimate:** $n\ge1$, $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{x:f(x)\tilde p(x)\ne0\}$, and the random variable
$$Y:=\begin{cases}f(X_1)\tilde p(X_1)/(Z_pq(X_1)),&q(X_1)>0,\\0,&q(X_1)=0\end{cases}$$
is integrable under $Q$. The support condition makes the value on $q=0$ immaterial to the target integral.

**Well-defined weights:** The reciprocal map $r(s)=1/s$ for $s>0$ and $r(s)=0$ for $s\le0$ is Borel. Its composition with $q$, multiplied by the measurable inputs, makes the piecewise weight and weighted integrand measurable ([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]], [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]).

**Procedure and output:** For each supplied draw $X_i$, set $Y_i=f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i))$ when $q(X_i)>0$ and set $Y_i=0$ otherwise. Return
$$\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i.$$
Separate variance and central limit claims require the corresponding weighted second-moment hypothesis.

Use the hypotheses and notation of [[thm-ordinary-importance-sampling-is-unbiased]]. Define
$$Y_i:=\begin{cases}f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i)),&q(X_i)>0,\\0,&q(X_i)=0\end{cases},\qquad \theta:=\int f\,d\pi,\qquad \sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}_Q(Y_1).$$
If $\mathbb E_Q[Y_1^2]<\infty$, then $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}$ has finite variance and
$$\operatorname{Var}_Q(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}})=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}=\frac1n\left(\frac1{Z_p^2}\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{f(x)^2\tilde p(x)^2}{q(x)}\,d\mu(x)-\theta^2\right).$$
This finite-sample conclusion is choice-free. For the central limit conclusion, let $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ be an IID sequence with law $Q$, and apply the estimator to its first $n$ draws for each $n\ge1$. If, in addition, AC holds, then
$$\sqrt n\bigl(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}-\theta\bigr)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2).$$
No finite variance or normal-limit claim is made when the weighted second moment is infinite.

Its weighted value is $Y=(Z_0/Z_1)R=\pi_1/\pi_0$, and finite summation gives $\mathbb E_{\pi_0}Y=(Z_0/Z_1)\mathbb E_{\pi_0}R=1$. Here $Z_1$ is used only to identify this mathematical random variable; it is not supplied to or computed by the raw-weight ratio estimator.

Apply [F2] to this formal weighted variable with mean $1$ from step 1.1. It gives $\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_n)=n^{-1}(\mathbb E_{\pi_0}[Y^2]-1)$. Since $\overline Y_n=(Z_0/Z_1)\widehat r_n$, rescaling gives $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat r_n)/(Z_1/Z_0)^2=n^{-1}(\sum_x\pi_0(x)(\pi_1(x)/\pi_0(x))^2-1)$.

The probability masses sum to one, so expanding the square gives $\chi^2(\pi_1\Vert\pi_0)=\sum_x\pi_0(x)(\pi_1(x)/\pi_0(x))^2-2\sum_x\pi_1(x)+\sum_x\pi_0(x)=\sum_x\pi_0(x)(\pi_1(x)/\pi_0(x))^2-1$. Substitution into step 2.1 proves the variance identity.

Let $\mathsf X$ be a finite nonempty set equipped with counting measure. For $a\in\{0,1\}$, let $w_a:\mathsf X\to(0,\infty)$ be a finite positive weight, define $Z_a=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}w_a(x)$, and define the probability mass function $\pi_a(x)=w_a(x)/Z_a$. For an integer $n\geq1$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent random variables with common law $\pi_0$. Define $R(x)=w_1(x)/w_0(x)$, $\widehat r_n=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^nR(X_j)$, and $\chi^2(\pi_1\Vert\pi_0)=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}\pi_0(x)(\pi_1(x)/\pi_0(x)-1)^2$. Then

$$\mathbb E_{\pi_0}[\widehat r_n]=\frac{Z_1}{Z_0},\qquad \frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_0}(\widehat r_n)}{(Z_1/Z_0)^2}=\frac{\chi^2(\pi_1\Vert\pi_0)}{n}.$$

The estimator uses only the finite raw-weight ratios $w_1(X_j)/w_0(X_j)$; the partition sums define the target ratio and probability laws but are not inputs to its computation.

Input a finite nonempty state space $\mathsf X$, an integer $K\geq1$, positive finite weights $w_0,\ldots,w_K:\mathsf X\to(0,\infty)$, positive integers $n_0,\ldots,n_{K-1}$, and, on a common probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, supplied random variables $X_{k,j}:\Omega\to(\mathsf X,\mathcal P(\mathsf X))$ for $0\le k<K$ and $1\le j\le n_k$. For each $k$, set $Z_k=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}w_k(x)$ and $\pi_k(x)=w_k(x)/Z_k$, a probability mass function on $\mathsf X$ and thus a probability measure on $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$. Require $\mathbb P(X_{k,j}=x)=\pi_k(x)$ for every $x\in\mathsf X$ and require the entire finite family $(X_{k,j})_{k,j}$ to be mutually independent. These exact draws are inputs, not outputs of this procedure; approximate Gibbs draws, correlated trajectories, and adaptively chosen bridges are outside its contract.

For each $k=0,\ldots,K-1$, compute $\overline R_k=n_k^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_k}w_{k+1}(X_{k,j})/w_k(X_{k,j})$. Return $\widehat R=\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}\overline R_k$. The procedure evaluates only raw-weight ratios; it neither computes nor requires any $Z_k$ as a numeric input.

derivations.claim: For each $k$, apply [F1] to $(w_k,w_{k+1})$ and the $n_k$ independent samples with common law $\pi_k$. With $r_k=Z_{k+1}/Z_k$, the stage mean $\overline R_k$ satisfies $\mathbb E[\overline R_k]=r_k$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\overline R_k)/r_k^2=\chi^2(\pi_{k+1}\Vert\pi_k)/n_k$. Since $\mathbb E[\overline R_k^2]=\operatorname{Var}(\overline R_k)+(\mathbb E[\overline R_k])^2$, it follows that $\mathbb E[\overline R_k^2]/r_k^2=1+\chi^2(\pi_{k+1}\Vert\pi_k)/n_k$. All moments are finite because $\mathsf X$ is finite and the weights are positive and finite.

Write $B_k=(X_{k,1},\ldots,X_{k,n_k})\in\mathsf X^{n_k}$. The blocks are independent finite-valued random elements, and $\overline R_k$ is a function of $B_k$. If $\mu_k(b)=\mathbb P(B_k=b)$, then for any functions $G_k$ of the respective blocks, independence and finite summation give $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}G_k(B_k)\right]=\sum_{b_0\in\mathsf X^{n_0},\ldots,b_{K-1}\in\mathsf X^{n_{K-1}}}\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}\mu_k(b_k)G_k(b_k)=\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}\mathbb E[G_k(B_k)].$$ Apply this first with $G_k=\overline R_k$ and then with $G_k=\overline R_k^2$. Thus $\mathbb E[\widehat R]=\prod_k\mathbb E[\overline R_k]=\prod_k(Z_{k+1}/Z_k)=Z_K/Z_0$, while $\mathbb E[\widehat R^2]/(Z_K/Z_0)^2=\prod_k\mathbb E[\overline R_k^2]/r_k^2$. Substitution from step 1.1 gives the stated product, and subtracting one yields the relative variance.

Let $\mathsf X$ be a finite nonempty set equipped with counting measure. For $a\in\{0,1\}$, let $w_a:\mathsf X\to(0,\infty)$ be a finite positive weight, define $Z_a=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}w_a(x)$, and define the probability mass function $\pi_a(x)=w_a(x)/Z_a$. For an integer $n\geq1$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent random variables with common law $\pi_0$. Define $R(x)=w_1(x)/w_0(x)$, $\widehat r_n=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^nR(X_j)$, and $\chi^2(\pi_1\Vert\pi_0)=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}\pi_0(x)(\pi_1(x)/\pi_0(x)-1)^2$. Then

$$\mathbb E_{\pi_0}[\widehat r_n]=\frac{Z_1}{Z_0},\qquad \frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_0}(\widehat r_n)}{(Z_1/Z_0)^2}=\frac{\chi^2(\pi_1\Vert\pi_0)}{n}.$$

The estimator uses only the finite raw-weight ratios $w_1(X_j)/w_0(X_j)$; the partition sums define the target ratio and probability laws but are not inputs to its computation.

derivations.claim: For $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\mathsf S^m$, the likelihood ratio is $\pi_1^{(m)}(x)/\pi_0^{(m)}(x)=\prod_{j=1}^m p_1(x_j)/p_0(x_j)$. Factoring the finite sum gives $1+\chi^2(\pi_1^{(m)}\Vert\pi_0^{(m)})=\sum_x\pi_0^{(m)}(x)(\pi_1^{(m)}(x)/\pi_0^{(m)}(x))^2=\left(\sum_{s\in\mathsf S}p_0(s)(p_1(s)/p_0(s))^2\right)^m=(1+\chi^2(p_1\Vert p_0))^m$.

Because $p_0\ne p_1$ and $p_0(s)>0$ at every $s$, at least one term in $\sum_s p_0(s)(p_1(s)/p_0(s)-1)^2$ is positive, so $\rho:=1+\chi^2(p_1\Vert p_0)>1$. Applying [F1] with $N$ draws gives relative variance $(\rho^m-1)/N$; the bound $(\rho^m-1)/N\leq\varepsilon$ forces $N\geq(\rho^m-1)/\varepsilon$. This establishes exponential growth for the stated one-stage estimator and makes no cost claim for bridge or other methods.
